column1: # perf/wasm_baselines.tsv — wall-time budgets for the wasm32-wasip1
# build under wasmtime. Sibling to `baselines.tsv` (which gates
# native rubyrs); same absolute-baseline policy + ratchet etiquette,
# scoped to the wasi shape because wasmtime startup + JIT + wasi
# syscall costs make native budgets irrelevant here.
# Format (tab-separated):
#   <workload-path>\t<max_wall_ms>\t<note>
# Only wall-time is gated. Peak-RSS isn't meaningful under wasmtime —
# the guest's linear memory is hidden behind a host VM and the
# `/usr/bin/time` numbers conflate wasmtime's runtime overhead
# with the guest's working set; without a stable lever there is
# no useful ratchet.
# Bumping etiquette: same as `baselines.tsv` — bump with a comment
# above the row explaining what grew and whether it was intentional;
# never "bumped to make CI green" silently.
# Initial calibration (Apple M-series, wasmtime 45.0.0,
# rubyrs.wasm release build):
#   cold_start.rb      ~10 ms (steady, first run ~180 ms with
#                              wasmtime's wasm-cache cold).
#   fizzbuzz_1m.rb     ~510 ms (M-series local).
# CI is on ubuntu-latest x86_64, where wasmtime + wasi-portable
# code typically run 1.5-2× slower than Apple Silicon native. Budgets
# below sit at ~3× the local M-series observed wall — that's the
# same headroom envelope the host `baselines.tsv` uses (~2× local
# to absorb CI's slowdown plus jitter), bumped slightly because
# wasmtime startup variance is larger than native's.
# Expect a re-cal commit if/when the wasmtime version pinned in
# CI bumps or the wasi-sdk shape changes.
